newsitem.title: USA: U.S. space-style ride for the public -- at $10,000.
newsitem.headline: U.S. space-style ride for the public -- at $10,000.

text.p: It will take you higher than Disney's Space Mountain and drop you farther than the Twilight Zone Tower of Terror.
The latest attraction planned for central Florida will give tourists a taste of space -- at an astronomical price of $10,000 for a day's training and about four minutes of weightlessness.

A roller coaster-like ride in a specially modified aircraft will simulate the weightlessness experienced by astronauts in orbit, officials from Casey Aerospace of Orlando said on Monday. Flights could start as early as spring of 1998.
"It's time to bring these types of experiences to the general public," said Casey president Ed Gibson, a former NASA astronaut. "Let people really know what it is like."
The thrill ride is probably not for those who would balk at the $136.74 price of a four-day Disney World pass.

The $10,000 price includes an education course to familiarize riders with the space programme. Participants will go home with a videotape of the zero-G experience and a NASA-style, light blue flight suit.

"At the end of the day you will have experienced the thrill of a lifetime," said Gibson, who spent 84 days in orbit aboard NASA's Skylab. "You will be part of a growing but relatively small group of people who know what it is like to break the bonds of gravity."

The ride will operate from a $50 million education centre adjacent to an airfield in central Florida. The aircraft will be similar to the one used by NASA to give astronauts a taste of weightlessness before they try the real thing on a mission.

It will provide about 30-second periods of weightlessness as it reaches the top of a steep climb before plunging about 4,000 feet (1,220 metres). During the 2-3 hour flight, the aircraft will make about 10 of these so-called parabolic manuevers.
Any more than that and the riders may find the experience stomach churning.
"We want people to come away from this with a very pleasant experience," said Gibson.

John Casey, chairman and CEO of Casey Aerospace, said funding for the project should be in place within 90 days. Selection of the aircraft's base and construction of the centre should get underway in early 1997.
In the meantime, those eager to ride the plane can secure a ticket with a $1,000 deposit.
